**Temperament**

The piano tuner came on a Tuesday, which my mother said was the only day he worked our side of the river. He was older than I expected, with hands that looked too thick for the job, and he carried a small black case that I assumed was full of tools but turned out to hold mostly felt wedges and a single tuning fork he rarely used. He said he could hear the A in his head. He'd been hearing it for forty years.

I was eleven and had been told to stay out of the way, so I sat on the stairs where I could watch through the banister. He took the front panel off the upright and I saw the inside for the first time: the hammers in their rows like a small, patient army, the strings running up and away, the dust that had settled on everything in the years since anyone had bothered to look.

He struck a key and then struck it again. He struck it maybe thirty times, turning a pin a fraction with his wrench, listening, turning it back. I remember thinking he had made a mistake, because the note sounded fine to me the first time and it sounded the same the thirtieth. But he kept at it, and eventually he moved on, and I understood that whatever he was hearing was happening in a room I couldn't get into.

At some point he noticed me and asked if I played. I said I was learning. He nodded like that was the correct answer and asked if I wanted to know a secret about the piano. I did.

"Every note on this thing is a little bit wrong," he said.

I didn't know what to do with that. He explained, in the way adults sometimes explain things to children—with more honesty than they'd use on other adults, because they assume it won't land. He said that if you tune a piano so that one chord is perfect, so that the intervals are as pure as the math says they should be, then the chords further away start to sound terrible. Sour. Wolves, he called them. There used to be keys you simply couldn't play in. So a few hundred years ago people agreed to spread the error out. Every interval would be nudged a hair off from true, so that none of them would be perfect and none of them would be unbearable. Equal temperament, he said. Everything slightly out of tune, so that everything could be played.

"So the whole thing is a compromise," he said. "And it's the best instrument anyone ever built."

Then he went back to work, and I went back to watching, and the afternoon went the way afternoons do.

I've thought about that conversation more than I've thought about most things adults said to me. Partly because it turned out to be true—I looked it up years later, and the math is exactly what he said, the fifths all shaved by a couple of cents so the circle closes. But mostly because it was the first time anyone had suggested to me that something could be good *because* it wasn't perfect, rather than in spite of it. That the wrongness wasn't a flaw that had been tolerated. It was the design.

I don't want to make too much of it. He was a piano tuner, not a philosopher, and he probably told that story to every kid on the stairs on every Tuesday for forty years. But I've noticed since then how many things work that way. How a friendship that has survived a long time is never quite in tune the way it was at the start, and how the surviving is the point. How a translation gives up something in every line so that the whole poem can cross over. How a marriage, from what I've seen of them, seems to be mostly people agreeing where to put the error so it doesn't all fall on one chord.

When he finished, he played something. Not a piece, just his hands walking around—a few chords in one key, then in another far away from it, then back. He was checking, I think, that no wolves had gotten in. It sounded like nothing in particular and it sounded completely right, and I remember being confused about how something could be both of those things.

He put the panel back on, and my mother paid him, and he told her the soundboard had a hairline crack that would probably never matter. "Probably never" was his phrase. He did not seem worried about it. He said most old pianos had something like that, and the ones that didn't had usually just been looked at less carefully.

I still don't play very well. I got to the point where I could read music slowly and get through the easier things, and then life did what life does. But sometimes I sit down at whatever piano is nearby—at a friend's house, in a hotel lobby—and I play a fifth, and I listen for the beat in it. It's there if you know to listen. A slow wobble, the sound of two frequencies that don't quite agree, agreeing to go on anyway. Most people never hear it. Most people shouldn't have to.

I think about him hearing that A in his head for forty years. A fixed point in a world of tempered intervals. I wonder if it was a comfort or a burden, carrying around the one true note in a job that was entirely about distributing untruth evenly. I suspect it was both, the way most things are. I suspect he would have said that was fine.

The piano is still in my mother's house. Nobody has tuned it since. It has gone, by now, the way of all untended things—some notes sagging, some holding, the whole slightly more wrong than it was designed to be. But you can still play it. You can play it in any key.
